# Keeping shots in one world

Shots generated one at a time drift apart. What holds them together:

- **People and recurring props are project Elements.** Reuse a fitting card or make one
  with `voyager cast create`: a hero portrait, a full-body image and a short description
  of what stays true in every look (face, hair, build, wardrobe; never the medium). For
  photoreal drama, prompt the hero as "a photo of an actor" on plain grey, not a
  "character sheet" (stiff CG); full turnarounds can make a model duplicate the character.
  Put every photo the user supplies on the card (up to 64, the clearest front portrait as
  hero); a real person's likeness comes only from their photos. Props and products go
  alone on a plain background, from the user's photos when they have them. `voyager cast
  from-model` makes a card from a `.glb`.
- **Pass `cast` with the element IDs and the project directory on every image and video
  estimate and run that shows them**, retakes included. Voyager attaches the photos and
  returns each one's label; write each visible element's identity using those labels.
  `voyager cast models` lists which routes take a card's references; `voyager cast check`
  is a paid second opinion on a still's likeness; never claim a match nobody checked.
- **Places** come from one design: an empty three-quarter location plate in the look,
  showing two walls and depth, no people. Cite it as the place's design and geography,
  never its framing or first frame.
- **The scene state** changes only when the story changes it: who sits or stands where,
  relative to the set piece and each other ("Tom at the table's far end, on Ana's left");
  set pieces, their state and props; the light; the side of the 180° line the camera keeps
  to. Open each prompt with its part of that state, and check reverses against it: what a
  viewer reads beats any camera geometry that explains a flip away.
- **An occupied scene anchor and named setups**: once a scene's people are placed, one
  frame with everyone at their marks and scale, and the camera setups the scene reuses
  (the wide, each over-the-shoulder, each close-up), so later shots come from the same
  coverage.
- **The subject the audience follows is unmistakable** in every shot: a colour or
  silhouette nothing else in the frame shares (the red car in grey traffic, not a grey
  car among grey cars), described the same way in every prompt, so wides and overheads
  still read.
- **Each shot's entry and exit state**: what has happened by its end (the glass is empty,
  the door now open), which take is the approved one, and which later shots were made from
  it, so a correction is carried to everything downstream.
- **One style key** (a frame and a few words) carries the look across every prompt, and it
  wins over a photo reference: a frame drifting toward a photo's realism is a failed take.
- **Compare before spending on motion**: keyframes, previs frames or a scene's draft takes,
  side by side in cut order as a script supervisor would: someone appearing, vanishing or changing seat or side, a prop gone or
  moved, a changed set piece, an angle that can't be the same place, a flipped eyeline.

Between two shots, the viewer either sees a cut or the same shot continues; a model's
duration limit decides where a generation ends, never where a shot ends.

- **Across a cut, carry the state, not the frame**: generate the next shot from its own
  references with the changed state in words ("her coat is now wet; the door behind her is
  open"). The previous shot's last frame drags its composition into the new angle.
- **Across a continuation, carry the motion**, in this order: one longer generation; the
  model's own extension (Seedance 2.5; Veo 3.1 for Veo-made clips), joined with an
  untrimmed straight cut; the kept take's last seconds as a video reference; first and
  last frames, generated about a second longer than needed and cut while still moving,
  since these takes settle onto their last frame; the last frame alone. A continuation's prompt opens on the
  action under way ("Continuing: the camera is already dollying in"), with no one entering
  who is already in frame.
- **A move through several places** is built from segments joined inside a place, never at
  a crossing (a dive is skim and dive in, then glide and breach). Write each change of
  place as the camera's path, not speed verbs whose blur hides a scene swap. Check each
  segment before extending from it, and retake only the one that fails.

# Model-specific prompting

Read the section for the model you chose before its first prompt; the general rules are in "Writing prompts" in SKILL.md.

## MiniMax H3 and H3 Max

[H3 prompt-writing
skill](https://github.com/MiniMax-AI/MiniMax-H3/tree/main/skills/h3-prompt-writing). On
fal, cite `Image 1`, `Video 1`, `Audio 1`, not `<Picture 1>`. `prompt_expansion_mode`
`disabled` sends your prose unchanged; the other modes rewrite it. MiniMax's labelled
format puts the picture in `integrated_multimodal_description:` with `[Shot 2] At
00:03.500, the camera cuts to …` and camera as type, amplitude and speed ("pushes in with
small amplitude at slow speed"); ambience in `overall_soundscape:`; score in
`non_diegetic_music:`, where `N/A` means no music. Speakers get IDs, `(S1)`, and lines go
in `<d>[English] exact words</d>`. Reference mode has six sections: an image cited inside
a `<Subject N>` definition supplies that subject, while a standalone image becomes a
target frame whose viewpoint the take copies. `target_audio_url` replaces the whole
soundtrack. A video reference's sound is not a voice reference: bind a voice once, and when
its original sound leaks into the take, set `retention_analysis` to `reference`, not
`fully_copy`, and say not to copy the original signal.

## Seedance 2.5

[Seedance 2.5 prompt guide](https://docs.byteplus.com/en/docs/ModelArk/2607689) (its FAQ
fixes known failures); the page renders in the browser, its Markdown in
`window._ROUTER_DATA` (`curDoc.MDContent`). On fal write `@Image1`, `@Video1`, `@Audio1`
by position in each list; upload subjects in order of first appearance, or it swaps
characters, and define each once ("Define the woman in the red raincoat in @Image1 as
Mia"). Order: asset mapping, one summary sentence, beats as contiguous whole-second ranges
(`0-3 seconds: …`, never fractions or gaps), then what stays constant. Dialogue in `{}`
with its language (`says in English {I'm not coming back.}`), effects in `< >`, music in
`()`. The `task` (reference, editing, extension) must match the prompt: "Strictly edit
@Video1: from 4-6 seconds, change …; leave the rest unchanged", "Extend @Video1 forward",
never "reference @Video1" for those. Use `voyager models show bytedance/seedance-2.5/reference-to-video --json` for draft resolution and completion limits. Stubborn music needs an audio policy, repeated per
shot, naming the excluded forms (score, melody, synth, drone, stinger). In long takes,
repeat two or three fixed identifiers at later beats. Intense emotion words can make eyes
glow ("normal human eyes"). An audio edit re-renders the picture and can shorten it by
about 0.4 s (8n+1-frame sources keep their length): for an
audio-only change, compare against the original and keep its picture if that's better.
Known fixes: remove subtitles from a reference video, since they override a subtitle ban;
reword water, wave or echo words when they bring bubbling or whistling; for a
mixed-language edit, give the full timed target script with every line translated.

Drafts' host refuses realistic faces on every plan. With photoreal Elements, Voyager substitutes a full 480p render (no `draft_id`) on Ultra/GigaMax; other plans refuse before sending. Even Ultra can refuse. If Seedance blocks realistic reference faces, never resend: offer the error's named models, a stylized Element or no face reference.

Seedance 2.5 (`task: "reference"`, `generate_audio: true`), with directly supplied images in upload order:

```text
@Image1 is Mia (red raincoat, short black bob); @Image2 is Leo (navy coat, curly brown hair); @Image3 supplies the station platform's layout, not its framing.
Mia and Leo await a train, realistic drama, three hard-cut shots.
0-4 seconds: Wide shot, Mia stands left of the bench, Leo right, both facing the tracks. <distant train horn> Train sounds only; no music.
4-8 seconds: Hard cut to track-side medium two-shot; Mia turns toward Leo. Mia says in English {It's our train.} Only her line and train sounds; no music.
8-12 seconds: Hard cut to Leo close-up, looking left toward Mia. <brakes hiss> Train sounds only; no music.
Keep faces, coats, marks and layout consistent. Audio policy: only the named dialogue and train sounds; no music, BGM, score, melody, synth, ambient pad, drone or stinger. No subtitles.
```

## Kling 3.0 and O3

[Kling VIDEO 3.0 guide](https://kling.ai/quickstart/klingai-video-3-model-user-guide);
fal's `o3` is 3.0 Omni. Direct multi-shot with `multi_prompt`; read `voyager models show fal-ai/kling-video/v3/pro/image-to-video --json` for shot controls and limits. References are `@Image1` and
`@Element1` (Kling's `elements`, filled from a card). Dialogue: one label and voice per
speaker, the action before the line, a linking word between turns (`[Character A: Agent,
raspy deep voice]: "where is the truth?" Immediately, [Character B: …]`), lowercase
English on fal; languages beyond Chinese, English, Japanese, Korean and Spanish come out
in English. Read `voyager models show fal-ai/kling-video/o3/pro/video-to-video/edit --json` for source-audio handling. O3 generation defaults to no audio, and neither O3 edit nor O3 video-reference generation makes new sound (`keep_audio` keeps the source's); check the exact variant before relying on it. For a fixed voice, check `voyager models show fal-ai/kling-video/create-voice --json` for recording limits, create one and bind it to the element; don't re-describe its tone, and
don't use native `<<<voice_1>>>` tokens on fal. Write "No background music"; only v3 has a
`negative_prompt`.

## Kling 4.0

After a Seedance face refusal, offer H3 / H3 Max or Kling 4.0. On `kling/v4/reference-to-video`, `cast` maps Mia/Leo to `@Element1`/`@Element2`; `start_image_url` supplies the approved platform wide; `multi_prompt` uses integer durations (no `shot_type` or `generate_audio`):

```text
duration: 12
multi_prompt:
  - duration: 4
    prompt: 'Wide shot, night-platform drama. @Element1 is Mia in a red raincoat, left of the bench; @Element2 is Leo in a navy coat, right. Both face tracks. Train horn only. No background music.'
  - duration: 4
    prompt: >-
      Hard cut to medium two-shot from the track side. Mia @Element1 remains left of the bench, Leo @Element2 right. Mia turns toward Leo. [Character A: Mia, quiet clear voice]: "it's our train." Only dialogue and train sounds. No background music.
  - duration: 4
    prompt: 'Hard cut to close-up of Leo @Element2 looking left toward Mia @Element1. Both keep their marks. Keep faces, coats and platform layout consistent. Brakes hiss only. No background music. No subtitles.'
```

## Veo 3.1

[Veo best
practices](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/video/best-practice).
One focused moment per clip; for image-to-video, describe only motion and camera. Speech
goes after a colon without quotes (`The detective says: Your story has holes.`), since
quotes can render as text. `negative_prompt` takes nouns (`wall, frame`); reference-to-video has no negative field.
Reference-to-video has no label syntax: describe the images in prose; `voyager models show fal-ai/veo3.1/reference-to-video --json` lists reference limits.
Timestamped beats (`[00:00-00:02] …`) suit two to four shots of one scene. Extension takes
clips within the limits in `voyager models show fal-ai/veo3.1/extend-video --json`; a voice carries on only if audible in the last second. Gemini API
Veo previews have shut down; use another provider offered by the catalog.
`auto_fix` rewrites a prompt that fails policy; check the chosen variant's model card for its default, since a changed result may not reflect
your prompt; a take blocked over audio processing
isn't charged, so retry it first.

## Gemini Omni Flash

[Omni guide](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/omni). It cuts between shots unless
told "single continuous shot, no scene cuts", and picks its own soundtrack unless you
describe one. No negative field: write "No dialogue. No background music." Speech after a
colon, unquoted. It renders legible text, so spell out a needed sign. References bind as
`<IMAGE_REF_0>` from zero. Edits are short and end "Keep everything else the same." It silently ignores the audio in video references. `voyager models show google/gemini-omni-flash --json` lists audio-reference and regional edit restrictions.

## Wan 3.0

[Wan 3.0 prompt
guide](https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/model-studio/wan3-video-generation-prompt-guide).
"One continuous shot" on the first line for a single take; "hard cut" or "dissolve"
between shots. `Image N`, `Video N`, `Audio N` are numbered separately, each scoped ("Only
reference the colour and lighting of Image 2"). Write "No dialogue." or it adds some; end
with "Negative prompt list:" naming only unwanted items. For an exact shot list or
verbatim dialogue, compare a take with prompt expansion off.
`voyager models show alibaba/wan-3.0/reference-to-video --json` lists reference combinations, duration caps and input billing. Fal has no Wan edit or extend endpoint, so Alibaba's edit and extend wording is unverified there.

## FLUX 3 Max

[FLUX 3 video prompting](https://docs.bfl.ml/guides/prompting_video_overview.md). One
flowing paragraph for a single take, sound last; several shots as `SHOT ONE: … HARD CUT.
SHOT TWO: …`. Its default high `reasoning_level` can add a cut to a single shot; `low`
makes that less likely. An off-screen line needs a `voiceover` cue, or it may be drawn as
text.

## LTX 2.5

[LTX prompting
guide](https://docs.ltx.io/api-documentation/implementation-guides/prompting-guide.md).
Flowing prose for simple shots, screenplay style for dialogue or several beats; rewrite
imported Kling or Seedance tags. It adds no pauses: write "a beat of silence" or set the
duration, which a last frame requires.

## Watch and listen to a clip

Use this only when the task needs evidence beyond local technical checks.

| Question | Approach |
| --- | --- |
| Layout, text, framing or a still | Extract a labelled contact sheet and inspect it: `voyager media frames clip.mp4 --output review/frames-v1 --times '[0,2,4,6,8,10,12]'`. |
| Loudness, black frames, silence or duration | `voyager media review clip.mp4 --json` measures the file locally; it does not watch motion or listen to the soundtrack. |
| What was said | `voyager speech transcribe clip.mp4 --local --output transcript-v1` writes word timings locally. A transcript does not establish tone, music, SFX or lip-sync. |
| Fine motion: lip sync, mouth shapes, hands, small text | A hosted review sees about one frame a second (its job's `coverage` says so); if appropriate, check locally with a dense strip: `voyager media frames clip.mp4 --output review/lips-v1 --around '[3.2]' --window 1 --step 0.04`, adding `--crop` for the face. |
| Motion over time, audio/video sync, or how music, voice and SFX sound | Ask a video+audio understanding model through `voyager models run`, as below. This is a paid upload. |

For an audio-only recording, make a small temporary MP4 with a static picture and
its original audio, then use that clip.

### Hosted understanding

The outer `model` is a fal endpoint; the downstream model belongs in native `input`.
The downstream Google name does not choose Google-key billing. Check the live schema
with `voyager models show openrouter/router/video --refresh --json` and inspect
`voyager models estimate --input @.voyager/request.json --json` before spending. A null
estimate means unknown cost, not free.

Save this with your other working files as `.voyager/request.json`; a relative `$file` path
would resolve from that folder, so name the video by its absolute path:

```json
{
  "model": "openrouter/router/video",
  "input": {
    "model": "google/gemini-3.8-flash",
    "video_urls": [{ "$file": "/absolute/project/exports/demo.mp4" }],
    "prompt": "Describe the motion and what you hear, including music, voice and SFX. Is the sound synchronized with the picture? Give approximate times and distinguish observations from uncertainty.",
    "reasoning": true,
    "max_tokens": 1500
  }
}
```

```sh
voyager models estimate --input @.voyager/request.json --json
voyager models run --input @.voyager/request.json --json
voyager jobs wait JOB_ID --timeout 60 --json
voyager jobs result JOB_ID --json
```

Read the returned JSON result file's `output` and `usage`, and the job's `coverage.summary`:
how many frames the model saw, how far apart and at what detail.

### Billing and limits

**Verified October 15, 2026:** `openrouter/router/video` with
`google/gemini-3.8-flash` works on **Voyager credits without a personal fal key**,
and on the user's own **FAL key**. Voyager's provider order chooses the payer;
the downstream model does not require the user's Google or OpenRouter key.
Read the estimate's `payer`, `billing` and `route` and the job's actual `served`
connection.

Prefer one clip per request
when source identity matters. Keep `reasoning: true` for this
model.

Voyager allows up to 512 MiB per file,
but the selected endpoint/model can impose a lower limit. Earlier tests (September 18,
2026) completed a 50 MB request; a 115 MB upload succeeded but inference hit a downstream
Google AI Studio 20 MB expanded-request limit inside the router. That is not a 20 MB
video-file limit. Do not assume native
Google sampling or processing controls exist in the router's schema.

---
name: make-ai-video
description: "Generate video shots, ads and commercials from prompts or images, or restyle existing footage with Voyager models; storyboard and assemble films."
applications:
  - id: moda
    role: primary
  - id: blender
    role: alternative
  - id: resolve
    role: alternative
  - id: ffmpeg
    role: fallback
  - id: remotion
    role: alternative
voyager:
  schemaVersion: 1
  design: optional
---

For motion, sound or sync checks beyond local measurements, read [Watch and listen to a clip](references/understanding.md).

## What this skill is for

Generated video, from single shots, ads and social clips to story films, and restyled
footage the user supplies: planning, generating, checking and assembling. Captured-room
tours start in [room-to-video](../room-to-video/SKILL.md), software demos in
[make-product-demo](../make-product-demo/SKILL.md), animated type and graphics in
[make-motion-graphics](../make-motion-graphics/SKILL.md), and cutting footage the user
already has in [edit-video](../edit-video/SKILL.md).

## Working with the user

Infer what the brief and attachments already say. Ask only what would change the plan:
what it's for, its length and format, and the look. A fully described shot, or a product
with photos, needs no questions. State the plan in one line the user can correct.

Develop the look and test what's uncertain before committing the whole piece: look frames
when the look is open, a test shot or a draft scene when the approach is untried. When
something the piece hinges on is open (who the main character is, the look), show a small
range, about three, rather than one guess; what the brief specifies is shown as described.
"Just make it" gets one strong choice and a first cut, made the way an expert would make
it: for a scene whose geography is the point, that includes the blockout.

The user's choices win: a workflow, model or editor they name is the one you use, and a
length they name is the length you deliver (add beats, or say why you'd go shorter). A script
or shot list they bring is carried out as written, with your expertise as brief notes
beside it ("Lena isn't established in the kitchen before shot 5; put her soft in the
background of shot 2?").

## Choosing a workflow

Practitioners pick the method by what the piece needs, and many pieces mix them. For a scene
where the same people act across several cuts, current practice is to generate the scene as
a sequence (a multi-shot generation from Elements, a location and a style key, with previs
when the staging is complex), rather than animating one opening still per shot; per-shot
keyframes are the choice when exact composition of each shot matters most. When the
geography is the point of the scene (a chase's turn and overshoot, a path past obstacles,
a camera circling a table, people facing each other across reverses), experienced AI
filmmakers recommend blocking it in Blender before generating anything, not as an
optional extra. The blockout itself is a few minutes of agent time and no generation spend;
with the restyled keyframes and video pass that follow, a previs-led scene took about twice
as long end to end as a direct generation. The generated scene then keeps the positions, paths and camera moves that prompts alone lose.
The blockout is a working step toward the finished film, not a detour from it: a user who
just wants a cinematic 20-second scene never has to review grey boxes, and gets a better
film because of them. Name the approach and why in the plan, and switch when the user asks.

- **Direct generation**, text or a supplied image to video: a single shot whose look is
  open, or one with a precise opening image the user already has.
- **Multi-shot scene in one generation.** Seedance 2.5 or Kling with timed hard cuts,
  directed as a sequence from Elements, a location and a style key: people, light and world
  hold together inside the scene. Whole-scene takes can still change an action or a detail
  between shots, and each shot's framing is less controlled.
- **Per-shot keyframes, then image-to-video.** Each opening frame is approved as a still,
  so composition is controlled shot by shot and a retake costs one shot; continuity across
  cuts rests on the stills matching, and people, light and staging drift between separately
  generated shots more than inside one scene generation.
- **Previs.** A Blender grey-box of the set, people and cameras, for many people, seating,
  a vehicle interior, complex blocking or a camera path: more setup, and geography that
  prompts alone don't hold. It plans the coverage and can feed keyframes or a multi-shot
  scene. Experienced AI filmmakers reach for a quick blockout whenever the action depends on
  where things are: a route (a chase's turn, a path past obstacles), a camera moving around
  a group, people facing each other across reverse angles. It takes minutes and no
  generation spend, and it is where "the police car overshoots the alley" or "she slides
  under the second beam" gets solved before any take is paid for.
- **References with Elements**, without a locked first frame: the model composes the shot
  from character, set and style references. Less control of composition; look development
  still helps.
- **Restyle supplied footage**: the user's video keeps its camera, timing and blocking and
  takes a new look.
- **Long-form or high-stakes films** (minutes long, a contest, a client): story, shot
  list, then generation scene by scene with the methods above.

What practitioners commonly start from, as a guide rather than a rule:

- **A single shot:** direct generation; a supplied image or exact opening goes in as the
  first frame; references when identity matters but composition doesn't.
- **A short ad:** product references and look development, a test of the product in action,
  then the shots or a compact sequence, with overlays and the edit. Products must keep their
  shape, label and material through the move; performance variants reuse the body and vary
  the hook, spokesperson or language; check the result on the delivery screen.
- **A short scene with several people or an action across cuts** (arrivals, a meeting, a
  chase): Elements for the people, a location plate and style key, then the scene as one or
  a few multi-shot generations; a Blender blockout first when who-stands-where or the route is the point (an 18-second
  chase with two animated cars and five cameras was blocked and rendered as an animatic in
  about five minutes). With
  photoreal people, use Seedance 2.5 when faces are allowed (Voyager credits: Ultra or
  GigaMax; never drafts; references can still be refused), otherwise MiniMax H3 / H3 Max
  or Kling 4.0 with Elements and timed shots.
- **A dialogue scene:** a stable cast and voices and the scene's staging, then either a scene
  generated with its own coverage or reusable wide, over-the-shoulder and close-up setups.
- **A story across scenes:** script and scenes, recurring assets and changing state, then
  generation by scene or shot and real post-production; previs where geography matters.
- **A restyle:** the source carries performance and camera; appearance references or an
  edited anchor frame guide the new look.

## Each workflow

Whatever the method, plan a scene the way an editor would cut it. A brief names
destinations ("it lands, people get off, they greet the aliens"); the scene is the beats
between them. Editors skip the dull middle of an action but show its turning points (the
ramp lowering, the first boot on the ground, the two groups seeing each other, the
approach), and a reaction or a look often carries the audience from one moment to the
next. Read the shot list as a sequence of cuts: where the jump from one shot's last frame
to the next shot's first would feel abrupt in a cinema, a beat is missing. Then make sure
each shot can show its beat happening: its opening frame comes before the key action
(seated before the toast, the blade sheathed before the draw, standing before he kneels,
the police car before the turn), because a still that already shows the result leaves
the clip nothing to do. The verbs in the brief are the actions the audience came to see, and the last one is the
payoff: give it a shot of its own that plays out fully and holds a moment before the cut.

### Per-shot keyframes, then image-to-video

Write the shot list, one line per shot: what we see, size and angle, the camera's move,
duration, sound. Make each opening frame with [make-image](../make-image/SKILL.md), with
the Elements in frame and the style key. Show the stills together in cut order, take the
user's notes, then animate exactly the approved files, spending the prompt on action and
camera. Derive reverse angles and close-ups from an approved wider still of the same set.
A single fully specified shot, a supplied image or a quick first cut can go straight to
video. Finish kept drafts without losing what was approved: complete a Seedance 2.5 draft,
or upscale the kept take or the locked cut; regenerating at a higher setting makes a new
take to approve again.

### Multi-shot scene in one generation

Pass the scene's Elements, location plate and style key as references, and write the scene
as timed shots with hard cuts (Seedance's whole-second ranges, Kling's `multi_prompt`).
Approved keyframes or previs renders can go in as references to pin the layout. From text
alone, a multi-shot generation holds the people loosely and lets the room change between
cuts (a table that grows, a window that moves); an occupied scene anchor, one still with
everyone at their marks, passed as a reference, is what keeps the room the same room. Draft at
low resolution, check every internal cut as you would a cut between clips, and finish the
keeper. Staging between shots can reset (an approach skipped, someone back at their first
mark), and a time-ranged edit barely changes staging: repair one bad shot by generating it
alone and splicing it in.

### Previs

A blockout is small: grey boxes and planes at real scale for the set, a plain proxy per
person or vehicle at its mark, a camera per setup at the lens you mean, and quick renders
of each camera. Experienced AI filmmakers treat it as the cheapest step of a staged scene,
not an extra. For grey-box blocking, marked proxies, coverage cameras and rendered
stills/animatics, follow [Blender's previs execution](../blender/SKILL.md#previs-execution). Blocked stills are often enough: restyle
them into keyframes with make-image editing, the render first and the style key and Elements
after it, keeping positions and perspective, or pass them as layout references to a
multi-shot scene. An animated grey-box is an animatic with exact timing and camera paths;
finished through a video-edit route (Seedance 2.5's editing task with the animatic as the
source video and the restyled keyframes as image references), it carries the blocked
camera moves, cuts and vehicle paths closely. Proxy people can carry stiff acting into the
take, so for performances the restyled stills usually lead and the animatic sets timing.

For a generated finish from authored 3D staging, continue with
[Restyle supplied footage](#restyle-supplied-footage); map inputs to the chosen endpoint's
editing/reference mode and [model prompting](#writing-prompts).

- Tell the editing model that video controls cameras, cuts and timing while images control appearance; state exact character counts and check reference prop placement to avoid duplicates.
- Rough mannequin limbs can transfer as stiff acting; avoid asking for natural performance and preservation of every pose in the same prompt.
- Send clean previs without labels or watermarks; generated cuts can shift by a frame and output dimensions can drift, so realign at assembly.
- Repair a defective shot as a targeted segment edit and splice back only its frames.

The video model copies the previs literally, so build it for that:
- Keep it coarse: one smooth volume per character or vehicle. Modelled detail comes back as geometry; it is not a fix for bleed-through.
- Give each character its own flat colour, close to its real main colour, and name the colour beside its reference in the prompt. Same-coloured proxies get swapped or doubled.
- Render flat and fully lit, with no mood lighting; the prompt sets night, rain or weather.
- Leave out anything floating or held (it comes back floating) and describe it in the prompt; keep stand-ins in contact with the ground.
- Depth reads as size: stage subjects side on when their sizes matter, and leave scale words ("giant", "tiny") out unless meant.
- Say in the prompt that the shapes mark only position and motion, and that their form comes from the references.
- Plan clips at the route's length (up to 30 s for Seedance 2.5 editing, 15 s of reference video for Wan 3.0 reference-to-video), with positions in metres and events on frames.

### References with Elements

Use a reference-to-video route (H3 Max, Seedance 2.5, Kling 4.0, Wan 3.0). Say what each
reference supplies and describe the framing, since no keyframe sets it. The take is the first look at the face: check identity, wardrobe and
silhouette through the whole clip, including its end.

### Restyle supplied footage

The source video supplies motion; a restyled anchor frame supplies the look. The user's
style reference is what you make the anchor from, never the only appearance input, and
image-to-video plus a motion prompt is a different workflow, not a substitute.
Seedance editing keeps much of the source's faces and hair; to swap in Elements, generating
from them usually holds identity better (Seedance 2.5's reference task with the clip as a
motion reference, or Kling v3 motion control for one performer).

1. Choose a route that takes the source video: Seedance 2.5's editing task; LTX
   render-to-real only for a photoreal target (its prompt starts with `3DREAL.`, and its
   output is smaller than fal's page says); H3 Max 3D-to-video for a 3D source with a
   photoreal target (pass the anchor, or it makes its own); Kling O3 edit when the
   source's sound must stay.
2. Trim and scale the source to the route's limits as a separately named derivative, each
   section opening on a representative frame.
3. Restyle each section's first frame with make-image editing, frame first and style
   reference second, keeping poses, perspective and object positions and leaving out the
   reference's own subject. A pose or prop shifted in the anchor drifts through the take.
4. Submit each section with its anchor. For Seedance, write an edit naming what stays
   ("Edit @Video1: restyle every frame to match @Image1. Keep the camera movement, timing,
   poses and composition of @Video1 unchanged.").
5. Check through the ending, where a take can freeze, change its camera path or revert to
   the source look.

For LTX 2.3 with Fal's 3DREAL adapter, verify the current
[model card](https://huggingface.co/fal/LTX-2.3-3DREAL-LoRA) and hosted schema before
trying that route.

Use `voyager models estimate` for the actual request’s price and measured timing before spending.

To match a reference clip instead, measure it: `voyager reference download` fetches an
online video. Crop away phone app bars, find cuts with the bundled ffmpeg's `scdet`
filter, and plan shot lengths and moves against the measured ones.

### Long-form or high-stakes films

Offer a plan, not a gate ("today story and look, tomorrow generation, then the edit and
sound"), as light as the piece allows. Keep plain notes in the project's
`films/<short-name>/`: the story, the shot list, the look, and per scene each shot's
prompt, inputs and the user's notes, so retakes rebuild from them.

- **Story** with the user: when the shape is open, offer two or three directions with the
  one you'd pick; keep the scope small and the turn photographable.
- **Shot list**: one clear action per shot, usually a change of size or angle across a
  cut, whether each shot cuts or continues, and each scene's state. Contest films are judged
  on story, look, technical execution and sound alike; contest shorts often cut quickly
  (a 3-minute short can run about 35 shots of 3–6 s), but pacing follows the piece.
- **When narration or a song drives the piece**, record or generate it first, measure it,
  and time the shots to it: lines to the images they pair with, cuts to the song's sections.
- **An animatic**, the boards or draft takes timed to the temp dialogue or music, shows
  pacing, repeated action and speed that a still strip can't.
- **Storyboards** are the keyframe strip or the previs frames. A sketch board, when wanted, is rough
  black-and-white pencil panels with arrows for camera moves, never fed to a video model.
- **Generation by scene**: draft, let the user mark keepers from a scene's drafts shown
  together, finish those, and report spend as you go.
- **Before presenting**, summarize what the cut shows (who wants what, how it ends) as a
  stranger would; where that misses the turn, re-cut first, then regenerate one shot.

## Keeping shots in one world

Shots generated one at a time drift apart. Before the second shot of a film, read [Keeping shots in one world](references/keeping-shots-in-one-world.md): project Elements for people and props, continuation between takes, and multi-place moves.

## Writing prompts

Direct each shot as a cinematographer would, with what these models need:

- **Starting positions stated** ("Mara at the counter, frame right; Jun wiping tables by
  the window behind her"), or models open on an empty frame or re-establish.
- **Detail sets the frame**: mention hands, the props on the table or another person's
  shoulder and you get that much frame, whatever shot size you name.
- **A few clear simultaneous actions**, shown by physical tells, not emotion words.
- **Camera move and subject pace in separate sentences**: speed words leak to everything
  in frame. Travel shows through changing surroundings or the subject's place in frame.
- **Physics stated**: where the light comes from, real-time motion unless slow motion is
  meant, weight, rigid things rigid, idle hands at rest.
- **Only what was asked**, and only this shot's people and props, since later characters
  leak in. Anything you added that draws a complaint comes out of prompt and stills.
- **Two or more people**: a count ("one Mara and one Jun; the references give identity
  only, not a layout"), relative heights, who stands where and holds what, and distinct
  silhouettes and colours.
- **No text for the model to write**; lettering goes on as an overlay. Write exclusions as
  the wanted state ("an empty, dry street"), never describing the unwanted thing, and
  exclude text, logos, watermarks, morphing, extra limbs, glow, flares and palette drift
  in the model's own form when unwanted.
- **Each reference's role in words** ("use image 2 only for her face and coat; draw the
  frame as loose line art, like image 1").
- **Sound written**, or the model improvises it; on shots cut together under one score, no
  music, in the model's own audio controls.

Before a model's first prompt, read its official guide for the exact version; `voyager
models docs` gives the fal schema and price, not prompting advice. Never copy one model's
syntax into another's prompt. With `cast`, write around the labels Voyager returns.

Per-model prompting notes (MiniMax H3, Seedance 2.5, Kling 3.0/O3/4.0, Veo 3.1, Gemini Omni Flash, Wan 3.0, FLUX 3 Max, LTX 2.5) are in [Model-specific prompting](references/model-prompting.md); read the one for your model before its first prompt.

## Choosing a model

`models list --kind KIND` filters declared output media and combines with `--query`
(or positional search words) and `--provider`; `--type` aliases `--kind`.
Kinds: `image`, `video`, `speech`, `sound`, `music`, `audio`, `3d`, `text`, `other`.
`audio` includes speech, music and sound; a model can match several kinds.
For example, `voyager models list --query kling --kind video --json` narrows a
family to video outputs. Follow `next_cursor`, including after an empty filtered
page, to finish searching fal's catalogue.

For “best/latest”, unfamiliar capabilities, or uncertain quality tradeoffs, use available web search to check current official model releases and endpoint docs. Translate the brief into short capability terms or synonyms for `voyager models list`; use `voyager models show MODEL --refresh --json` for the exact variant and `voyager models docs MODEL --json` for dated provider documentation.

No model is the answer for a product UI whose text must read: build it from real
screenshots or recordings with editable motion
([make-product-demo](../make-product-demo/SKILL.md)), never by animating a
screenshot or prompting a model to draw the interface; generate only the shots
without UI.

The creative preferences' video-model line or a model the user names decides. Otherwise
choose by the shot. `voyager models list --kind video --json` covers the long tail when the user names a model or the job needs something unusual; where it or an
estimate disagrees with this file, they win. A personal OpenAI key opens no video route.

- **Text to video:** Wan 3.0 for top text-only quality; FLUX 3 Max for cheap, fast,
  high-quality clips; MiniMax H3 for value, faces and dialogue.
- **Image to video, from a keyframe:** Seedance 2.5 for top quality; MiniMax H3 / H3 Max
  for value, speed, faces and lip-sync; Kling 4.0 for middle keyframes and timed beats
  at a fraction of Seedance's price (`kling/v4/image-to-video`).
- **Reference to video, without a keyframe:** Seedance 2.5 for many references and a
  cast held across shots when faces are allowed; Kling 4.0 for Elements and timed shots
  (`kling/v4/reference-to-video`); H3 Max for faces and up to nine Elements; Wan 3.0
  for several characters in one long take (vendor claim).
- **Video to video from previs:** Seedance 2.5 editing with the animatic and restyled
  keyframes, Wan 3.0 reference-to-video with the animatic as its reference video (up to
  15 s), or H3 Max 3d-to-video with the grey-box video. Seedance editing and H3
  3d-to-video gave our best previs results; Wan has no fal edit route.
- **Photoreal faces:** Seedance 2.5 on Voyager credits with Ultra/GigaMax or the user's
  own provider access; drafts never take realistic faces, and references can still be
  refused even on Ultra. Otherwise, or after a refusal, use H3 / H3 Max or Kling 4.0.
- **Off the frontier:** Kling 3.0, Veo 3.1, Gemini Omni Flash and Seedance 2.0 only when
  the user names them or needs a feature the frontier picks lack: Veo extension of a
  Veo clip, or Kling v3 motion control (the catalog has no v4 motion-control route).

A user who asks for a specific model gets it. H3 Max Turbo takes H3 Max's inputs for less;
1080P and Turbo run on fal, not Higgsfield. FLUX 3 Max's keyframes-to-video takes
frame-indexed anchors. LTX 2.5 reaches higher resolution and frame rates and drives a scene
from audio: `voyager models show lightricks/ltx-2.5/text-to-video/fast --json` lists
duration/resolution/frame-rate combinations; check `lightricks/ltx-2.5/audio-to-video/pro`
for the audio-driven limit.

Rankings move: check the Artificial Analysis [image-to-video](https://artificialanalysis.ai/video/leaderboard/image-to-video)
and [text-to-video](https://artificialanalysis.ai/video/leaderboard/text-to-video)
blind leaderboards. Kling 4.0 is not yet rated; its place here is for reference control.
`voyager models estimate` remains the price and payer truth for the actual request.

`voyager models list --provider fal --query "words" --json` narrows discovery to one provider. A `local:` model runs only on this computer: remove a conflicting provider pin, or use its `hostedAlternative` model ID to estimate a hosted run.

For price, payer and typical time, run `voyager models estimate` on the actual request; otherwise use that endpoint’s `measured_seconds` from `voyager models list` or observed job times, or call speed unknown.
Local video models (`voyager models list local --json`) run free on this computer and can take several minutes: tell the user up front, and keep chatting while it runs.

For supplied footage or people: a portrait plus speech (Sync v3 avatar, H3 Max lip-sync,
HeyGen Avatar 4); new speech in footage (Sync v3 lip-sync); a performance onto a character
(Kling v3 motion control); a masked region replaced (Wan VACE inpainting, which brings the
original back unless that area is greyed out first or `preprocess` is on); upscaling
(Topaz, SeedVR).

A Runway API key runs Runway's own models as `runway:<model>/<operation>` (`voyager models
list runway`), only on that key and never as a fallback or substitute. A BytePlus ModelArk
key, once enabled in Connectors → Providers, runs Seedance and Seedream natively as
`byteplus:<model-id>`; fal requests don't translate to it, and its dollar price is
unknown. It can't upload local videos, never falls back automatically, and a lost answer
or task ID leaves the job uncertain: never replay it.

## Generate, check, deliver

Start every generation from what the user approved (stills, references, previs frames),
never a rejected take, and
give each idea a short title so its takes share a file name. Submit every clip of an
approved batch before waiting on any, and carry an approved plan through to the finished
video: a job wait is not a stopping point. A request identical to an earlier one returns that
job (`reused`) and charges nothing: say so, and make a fresh take only if the user wants
one. Voyager handles provider fallback, so don't resubmit on another model yourself,
except once after a content filter refuses an allowed request: say which provider refused
(without guessing a trigger it didn't name), try another suitable model or revised
wording, and agree the next step with the user if that fails too. Keep the same `cast`
IDs; never relabel a card to get past a refusal.

Check every take before showing it: `voyager media review`, then frames about a second
apart through the last second (`voyager media frames`). First, that the shot's action
visibly happens (the water reaches the plant); then identity, hands, objects appearing or
vanishing, morphing, invented text, drift, floating motion, anything wrong for the period,
and the scene state; on an assembled cut, review also flags a move that pauses at a join.
Watch once with the sound off. A fault visible at normal speed is a blocker (trim, cover
or retake); one visible only frame by frame is polish. For motion, sync or sound frames
can't show, use [hosted understanding](../make-ai-video/references/understanding.md).

Retakes: repair one local fault in place; regenerate a shot with two or more faults or
broken motion, rebuilding the prompt from what it must show plus every correction the user
made. Change one thing at a time and judge it on two takes, extend from an approved
opening rather than re-rolling the move, and say what improved and what regressed.

Present each draft and the final with `voyager files present` under one deliverable name.

Cut in the user's chosen editor ([davinci-resolve](../davinci-resolve/SKILL.md),
[premiere-pro](../premiere-pro/SKILL.md), [capcut](../capcut/SKILL.md)); otherwise the
video engine as [edit-video](../edit-video/SKILL.md) describes, when `<voyager_environment>`
lists it as ready; otherwise `voyager media assemble`, never a hand-written FFmpeg concat. Don't silently switch from a
chosen editor. Trim unsteady heads and drifting tails (a continuation's join keeps its
motion); a reaction or insert can bridge a seam.

Sound comes in three layers: a continuous ambience bed with no silence between clips, the
effects that sell the action, then voice and score; sound overlapping a cut (J- and L-cuts
in `media assemble`) smooths joins. A piece you make gets a fitting score
([make-music](../make-music/SKILL.md)); a talking head gets none unless asked; a single
standalone clip can keep its own. Effects and mix: [make-sound](../make-sound/SKILL.md);
narration: [voiceover](../voiceover/SKILL.md). One person speaking to camera in a take of
up to 15 s can be native speech, listeners' lips closed (transcribe it and check the
words); a longer script, a chosen or cloned voice, or a presenter reused across pieces is
voiced first, then lip-synced. Exact lettering, logos, prices and claims go on as
overlays. Speaking videos for social get large burned-in captions unless the user says
otherwise; for vertical framing see [social safe
areas](../edit-video/references/social-safe-areas.md). To place a label on a moving
subject, `voyager media cutout` isolates it (name exactly one instance) and `voyager media
crop-alpha` reports its box.

## Pitfalls

- Models garble small text, so real app, website and dashboard screens come from
  make-product-demo; if the user insists on a model drawing them, say once the text won't
  be exact.
- A still with an unnoticed error becomes canon in every shot made from it.
- Each clip brings its own ambience, so sound jumps at every cut without a shared bed.
- Seating and screen sides flip across reverse angles even when faces hold.
- On routes without frame-indexed anchors, more than two keyframe stills in one generation
  fade into each other instead of moving.
- A drawn storyboard panel fed to a video model leaks its linework into the render, and a
  multi-panel board image is only a loose plot guide.
- Some H3 Max takes open squashed; `voyager media review` flags it, so trim the frames it
  names.
- H3 Max runs slightly longer than requested; trim to the asked length.
- Upscaling can invent detail, so look at the cut again after any upscale.
- Generated footage must not pass for evidence of a real event; label it as a
  visualization where viewers could mistake it.
